style.summary:
style of A: A is formal and procedural, with 'Uh, O_K' and 'so that's -', and frames the exchange in meeting-chair language about the agenda.
style of B: B is polite and deferential, answering 'Uh-huh. O_K.' and thanking A with 'Thank you for your information'.

A: A's procedural language ('the last thing on my agenda') gives A's manner the feel of a chair running the meeting.
A's formal register sets the terms of the exchange and makes A's requests sound like the expected format.
A's courteous tone is the kind that makes A's request for an update feel like an instruction.
B: B's polite acknowledgments keep the register cooperative and make B's contribution feel welcome.
B's thanks show B accepts A's framing, which places B in the position of responding.
B's deferential tone makes B's report appear as the answer A asked for.

A: Procedural language is a way of organising a turn, and B's readiness to report decides what is said. B controls the content of the meeting.
A formal register does not settle the format, since B's report determines what the meeting learns. The format is B's to fill.
A courteous request still depends on B's willingness to answer, so the instruction only works if B complies. B decides.
B: Polite acknowledgments are passive and do not change the agenda A sets. A's framing still governs the exchange.
Accepting A's framing means B responds within A's structure, not that B shapes it. A keeps the frame.
Deference makes B's report look like an answer, which reinforces that A is the one who asked. A holds the role of the requester.

content.summary:
content of A: A sets the agenda, saying the last item was an update on what Jose has been doing.
content of B: B has results from recent work to report and offers to share them.

A: A sets the agenda and names the subject of the update, so A determines what the meeting covers.
A's choice of the update on Jose as the last item shapes the substance of the meeting.
A's framing of the item as the last thing on the agenda defines the scope of the exchange.
B: B holds the results that the meeting is waiting for, so B supplies the substance.
B's offer to report the results of the last days makes B the source of new information.
B's report is the content of the exchange, which gives B influence over what is discussed next.

A: An agenda is procedural, and B's results are the content the agenda exists to hear. B's report, not A's agenda, determines what is learned.
Naming an update does not decide its substance, and B chooses what to present. B controls what is disclosed.
Defining a scope is a frame, and B's results fill it. The substance depends on B's report.
B: Holding results gives B information, but A asked for the update and so defined why it is reported. A's request frames the content.
Offering to report responds to A's request, so the subject of the report is still A's. A determines what is covered.
Being the source of new information matters only if the group uses it, and A decides how it is discussed. A keeps the authority over the topic.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: A opens the exchange, sets the agenda and hands the floor to B with an incomplete turn.
coordination of B: B takes the floor when offered and begins a thanks that trails off with 'because I -'.

A: A opens the exchange and manages the transition to the update, so A controls the sequence of the meeting.
A decides who reports and when, which gives A control over the order of items.
A's incomplete handover is what gives B the floor, so A controls the transition.
B: B takes the floor once A hands it over and begins a report, so B holds the next substantive turn.
B's trailing 'because I -' keeps B's turn open and signals more to come.
B's readiness to speak means B decides when the report starts.

A: Opening a meeting is procedural, and B's report starts whenever B chooses. B determines the timing of the substance.
Deciding who reports only sets the order, and B controls the content and length of the report. The order does not give A the content.
A handover depends on B accepting the floor, so the transition is B's to take. B controls whether it happens.
B: Taking the floor when offered is a response to A's handover, so A decides when B speaks. A keeps the transition in hand.
An open turn invites A to respond, and A can take the floor back. The choice to continue belongs to A.
Readiness to speak is limited by A's permission, and A sets the start of B's report. A controls the timing.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: A engages by asking for an update on another colleague's work, which shows interest in the progress of the group.
engagement of B: B engages by offering to report and thanking A, which shows willingness to contribute.

A: A's request for an update shows active interest in the colleague's work.
A's attention to what the group needs shows sustained involvement in the meeting's progress.
A's engagement with the agenda shows A is invested in keeping the meeting on track.
B: B's offer to report shows B is ready to contribute substantively.
B's thanks shows B is attentive to A's requests and responsive to them.
B's preparedness to present results shows B has been working and is invested in the outcome.

A: Asking for an update is a request that B answers on B's terms, so B decides how much interest is shown. B's response shapes the engagement.
Keeping the meeting on track is procedural, and B's report is the content that engages the group. B's contribution matters more.
Investment in the agenda is a claim A can make, but B's results carry the substance. The engagement that counts is B's.
B: Offering to report is a response to A's request, not an initiative B has taken. A's prompt is what drives the contribution.
Thanks are a polite reply and do not show that B is leading the engagement. A's request came first.
Preparedness shows effort, but A decides whether the results are discussed. A's engagement determines the use of the work.
